0044.event: The Lake Walkers takes its name from fossils found near ancient lake shores in Kenya, dating to about four million two hundred thousand years ago. The bones belong to very early members of the human family, creatures who still climbed with long arms yet walked upright on two legs. Their remains settled into lake mud and silt, where hippos and crocodiles also lived, and were preserved as the lake beds hardened into stone. Scientists read these fossils as a bridge between tree dwelling apes and ground walking humans. They did not know they were becoming us. They only knew the shore, the water, and the slow work of survival, one upright step at a time.
0044.announce: Here is a poem about the first walkers at the lakeshore: The Lake Walkers.
0044.title: The Lake Walkers
0044.piece:
I came down to the water where the tall reeds grew,
and heard soft splashing long before they came in view.
Half upright through the papyrus, through the sedge they went,
with arms that still remembered what the branches meant.
Climbing arms and walking legs, one body torn between
the trees it used to live in and the ground as yet unseen.
They waded where the hippos rolled, they drank, they fed, they played,
and left their bones in Kenyan mud, where time and silt have stayed.
They did not know the future. They only knew the shore.
But they were us already, walking, wanting more.

0443.event: The Village Age Ends marks the rise of the first cities, around five thousand years ago. From the Nile valley to the plains between the Tigris and Euphrates, from the Indus valley to the Yellow River, farming villages grew into walled towns and then into cities. With cities came kings, priests, scribes, markets, and armies. Writing was invented to count grain and goods. Laws were carved to govern crowds. The old life of small villages, where everyone knew everyone, gave way to streets, temples, and palaces. Civilization, with all its wonders and all its cruelties, had begun, and the human story would never be small again.
0443.announce: The following poem walks from the first planted seed to the first city wall: The Village Age Ends.
0443.title: The Village Age Ends
0443.piece:
From the Nile to the Yangtze, cities rose where villages stood,
and the first long chapter of the human story closed for good.
I stood upon a hill and looked across ten thousand years:
the first wild harvest, the first sown seed,
the first shaped pot, the first warm loaf, the first tame herd,
all of it leading here, to walls and crowded streets,
to kings and scribes and markets, to the humming of the town.
The wanderers had put down roots. The roots became fields.
The fields became cities. And I had walked each step beside them.
The village age was over. The story was just beginning.

1092.event: The Plague struck Athens in the year 430 before the common era, in the second year of its long war with Sparta. Crowded with refugees behind the city walls, Athens was ripe for sickness. The disease brought burning fever, red eyes, and a thirst no water could quench. Thucydides, the historian, caught it and lived, and wrote down what he saw: the temples filled with the unburied dead, the funeral pyres running out of wood, the laws of burial abandoned. The plague returned again and again over several years. It carried off a great part of the people, including Pericles, the statesman who had led Athens to its height. The city survived the plague, but something in its spirit did not.
1092.announce: A poem of the crowded city and the summer sickness: The Plague.
1092.title: The Plague
1092.piece:
It came with the summer, the sickness, from the crowded ships,
from the refugees packed inside the Long Walls.
I nursed my neighbors through it. I buried two of them myself.
Thucydides wrote it down: the burning head,
the red eyes, the thirst no water touched,
the bodies laid in the temples because the pyres ran out of wood.
Athens buried its dead without rites, without names.
The laws of burial, of decency, of the gods,
all of it went into the plague pits together.
Pericles lost his sons to it. Then Pericles himself.
The city survived. Something in it did not.

1926.event: The Comet of Conquest is Halley's Comet as it appeared over England in the spring of 1066. That autumn, Duke William of Normandy would invade and defeat King Harold at Hastings, but in April all England could do was stare at the burning star. Both sides read it as an omen. The English feared it foretold the doom of Harold. The Normans hoped it promised the triumph of William. The Bayeux Tapestry, sewn to tell the story of the conquest, shows frightened men pointing at the comet, with words in Latin saying they marvel at the star. The comet was only ice and dust swinging past the sun. But believed hard enough, an omen has a way of coming true.
1926.announce: Here is a verse about the burning star that both armies read as an omen: The Comet of Conquest.
1926.title: The Comet of Conquest
1926.piece:
It hung over England for a week,
Halley's Comet, blazing in the spring sky,
and everyone knew what it meant.
Everyone always knows what comets mean:
disaster, death, the fall of kings.
I stood in a Sussex field and watched the villagers
point at it with white faces.
The English said it foretold the doom of Harold.
The Normans said it foretold the triumph of William.
The Bayeux Tapestry sewed it into the story for all time:
men staring up at the burning star,
marveling, as the old Latin says, at the star.
It was only ice and dust, swinging past the sun.
But in 1066 it was an omen,
and omens, believed hard enough, have a way of coming true.

2744.event: The Cantor's Thousand Songs remembers Johann Sebastian Bach at work in Leipzig, Germany, around 1725. Bach had taken the post of cantor at the church of Saint Thomas two years before, and with it the duty of providing new music for every Sunday and feast day. In those first years he wrote a fresh cantata nearly every week, music of staggering craft poured out like daily bread. His choir boys grumbled at the difficulty. His congregation dozed through much of it. Almost no one in Leipzig understood what was happening in the organ loft. In time the world would call him one of the greatest composers who ever lived, but in 1725 he was only a tired church musician with ink on his cuffs, writing for God.
2744.announce: The following poem stands in the church loft beside the tired cantor: The Cantor's Thousand Songs.
2744.title: The Cantor's Thousand Songs
2744.piece:
I was there in the Thomaskirche loft,
a nobody with ink on his cuffs,
watching a tired man with failing eyes
hand out new music as if it were nothing:
a fresh cantata every single week,
as regular as bread, as wild as prayer.
The choir boys grumbled at the hard passages.
The congregation half slept in the pews.
And none of them knew. But I knew.
He was writing for God and for nobody,
a thousand songs poured out like rain
on a town too small to hold them,
with all of heaven leaning in to listen.

3311.event: The Unsinkable Sinks tells of the RMS Titanic, lost in the North Atlantic in April 1912. The largest ship afloat, on her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York, struck an iceberg late on the night of April 14. She sank in the early hours of April 15, taking about fifteen hundred souls with her, in water cold enough to kill within minutes. Millionaires and steerage passengers faced the same dark. The band played on. The nearby Carpathia raced through ice fields to gather the survivors from the lifeboats at dawn. Newspapers had called the ship unsinkable. The sea answered otherwise, and the twentieth century learned its first great lesson in pride.
3311.announce: A poem for the night the sea answered the press releases: The Unsinkable Sinks.
3311.title: The Unsinkable Sinks
3311.piece:
The Titanic struck the iceberg near midnight,
and the unsinkable ship went down before dawn.
I was not aboard, but I stood on the deck of the Carpathia
when the lifeboats came alongside, and I heard the silence.
Fifteen hundred gone in the freezing dark,
the band still playing, the rich and the poor alike.
The century learned its lesson in a single night:
pride floats only until it meets the sea.
No press release was ever proof against the cold.
The great ship sleeps now, two and a half miles down,
and every sonar ping still spells the same word: listen.

3925.event: The Ship of Dreams is the film Titanic, released in December 1997. Directed by James Cameron, the three hour romance set aboard the doomed liner became the highest earning film ever made up to that time, passing every record before it. Audiences wept in packed theaters, returned to watch it again, and made its love theme one of the most played songs in the world. It won eleven Academy Awards, tying the all time record. The film did for 1912 what no history book had done: it put millions of living people aboard the ship, made them love two young passengers, and then made them watch the ocean take them. The ship of dreams sailed into history twice.
3925.announce: Here is a poem about the film that made the whole world weep for 1912: The Ship of Dreams.
3925.title: The Ship of Dreams
3925.piece:
Cameron built the ship again,
three hours long, and filled it with the young,
and the world went aboard and wept for 1912.
I saw it twice in the opening week,
the crowd around me sobbing at the stern.
The ship of dreams sailed into box office history,
the biggest film the world had ever seen.
A poor boy shouts from the bow that he is king of the world.
A poor girl lets the cold sea keep her heart.
Love stories, it turns out,
can float even the heaviest ships.

3944.event: The Night the Computers Didn't Break is the story of the Y2K scare, which ended on January 1, 2000. For years, experts had warned that computer systems storing years as two digits would fail when the calendar rolled from 99 to 00, reading 2000 as 1900. Banks, airlines, power grids, and governments spent vast sums rewriting code and testing systems. Survivalists stocked food. Preachers named the date. Then midnight came, the clocks turned over, and almost nothing happened. A few minor glitches flickered and died. Humanity had spent billions preparing for an apocalypse and bought itself an ordinary New Year. It remains the most expensive scare that never happened, and proof that preparation works.
3944.announce: A poem about the midnight that arrived like any other midnight: The Night the Computers Didn't Break.
3944.title: The Night the Computers Didn't Break
3944.piece:
They told us the world would end at midnight,
every banker, every coder, every screen gone dark,
the planes would fall, the lights go out,
because some tired programmer wrote the year with two digits.
I walked the server rooms and saw the fear,
the money spent, the keyboards worn to bone.
Then the clock turned over, clean and clear,
and nothing broke at all. We had outgrown
our own small prophecy of doom that year.
The costliest fix in history, and it worked.
Sometimes the end of the world we prepare for
is only the shadow of the work we did.

2658.event: Watteau Is Born marks the birth of Antoine Watteau in October 1684, in Valenciennes, France. He would become the painter of the fete galante, dreamy scenes of elegant parties in parks and gardens, lovers in silk among the trees, music playing as the light fades. His most famous canvas shows a pilgrimage to the island of love itself. Watteau painted beauty with a thread of sadness running through it, as if he knew the party was already ending. He died at only thirty six, his health broken, but his shimmering world of grace and longing shaped French painting for a century. The parties he painted never quite happened, which is why we still remember them.
2658.announce: A short verse for the painter of parties that never quite happened: Watteau Is Born.
2658.title: Watteau Is Born
2658.piece:
A child of Valenciennes that year,
Watteau, who painted the parties dear:
gallant fetes in the evening air,
lovers who were never quite there.
I wandered through his painted park
and felt the daylight lose its spark.
Silk and music, trees and stone,
beauty touched with the unknown.
He was gone by thirty six, they say,
but the sad sweet parties never went away.
Beautiful, fleeting, slightly sad:
the happiest paintings ever had.

0958.event: Pyramids at Nuri stands in Nubia, in what is now Sudan, where the kings of Kush built their tombs around 650 years before the common era. The Kushites, the black pharaohs who had once ruled all of Egypt, raised steep sided pyramids at Nuri near their capital Napata. They were not copies of the great pyramids of Giza. They were smaller, sharper, and their own, built by southern hands for southern kings. Masons set capstones over burial chambers cut deep into the rock, and the dead were laid to rest with the goods of two kingdoms. Egypt's glory did not die. It moved south, up the Nile, and built itself again in stone.
0958.announce: The following poem walks among the steep pyramids at dusk: Pyramids at Nuri.
0958.title: Pyramids at Nuri
0958.piece:
Steep and sharp they rose above the Nubian sand,
the pyramids of Kush, raised by a southern hand.
I watched the masons set the final capstone high
at Nuri, where the old kings sleep beneath the sky.
Not copies of the north, but their own design,
sharp against the dusk, stone upon stone in line.
I walked among the tombs as the shadows grew long and deep.
The south remembers what the north forgot to keep.
Two kingdoms in the grave goods, one river running through,
and glory, born again, in a southern hue.
